To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) firms use formal governance and selection of the exchange partner as two distinct and complementary mechanisms to cope with interfirm control issues, (ii) the choice of governance design is influenced by appropriation concerns and coordination requirements, while partner selection is influenced by appropriation and dependence, and (iii) the effects of appropriation and dependence are moderated by prior experience with the exchange partner.

(1) appropriation concerns, coordination problems and dependence influence governance decisions and partner selection, and (2) partner selection is used to reduce the need for formal governance, but only in cases of high appropriation concerns.

firms’ partner selection and governance design choices depend on the nature of the exchange, on the partner selection efforts of the exchange partners, and on their prior experiences with the partner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interplay between partner selection, governance design and prior experiences in interfirm relationships.
the interplay of partner selection and governance design in the management of interfirm relationships.
the question of whether and how interfirm relationships can be governed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
firms use partner selection to identify the most appropriate exchange partner and then use a governance mechanism to control this partner.

partner selection and governance are both used by firms to deal with interfirm control and coordination problems, but the former is used more for dealing with appropriation problems, while the latter is used more for coordinating the relationship.
partner selection is not a substitute for formal governance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we develop a structural model to analyze firms’ partner selections and governance design in managing interfirm relationships and test this model in the context of information technology outsourcing relationships.

the choice of partner selection and governance design in a dyadic relationship is a joint decision, and the choice is influenced by the same control problems that affect the choice of governance in a relationship.
firms’ partner selection and governance design are driven by different control concerns, and that firms use both partner selection and formal contracts to cope with interfirm control concerns.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the governance design and partner selection activities of firms are interlinked and jointly influenced by control problems and prior experience with the exchange partner.
firms use partner selection to reduce control costs, and that this partner selection activity is influenced by appropriation concerns.
firms’ partner selection and governance choices are driven by different factors.
